To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a novel subcloned cell line, CRI-G1 RS, has increased vulnerability to mitochondrial toxins and oxidative stress compared with its parental cell line, CRL-1544 RR, due to a defect in Nrf2-mediated antioxidant gene expression.

a novel cell line, CRI-G1 RS, which is more susceptible to mitochondrial dysfunction than the parental line, CRI G1 RR, exhibits a distinct gene expression profile that is characterized by (1) decreased expression of Nrf2/ARE target genes and (2) increased expression of chaperones and β cell specific genes.

(1) differential vulnerability to mitochondrial and/or oxidative stress in two clonal cell lines was associated with differential expression of genes that are known Nrf2 transcription targets, (2) differential vulnerability to these stresses was not associated with differences in expression of genes involved in apoptosis, and (3) the newly isolated cell line represents a useful model for studying the role of endogenous antioxidants in glucose sensing and insulin secretion by pancreatic β cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular basis of mitochondrial and oxidative stress vulnerability in a neuroendocrine cell line.
the molecular mechanisms that underlie the vulnerability to oxidative and mitochondrial stress and the ability to respond to these stressors.
identifying the molecular basis for differential vulnerability to mitochondrial and metabolic stress in a neuroendocrine CRI cell line.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the molecular profile presented here enables identification of individual genes that shape vulnerability to oxidative stress.
the molecular profile presented here would enable identification of individual gene or gene clusters that shapes vulnerability to mitochondrial dysfunction.
this study provides new insights into the molecular mechanisms of mitochondrial and oxidative stress and their relationship to cell fate determination.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified a cell line (CRI-G1-R5) that has an increased susceptibility to oxidative and mitochondrial stress.
the CRI-G1 cells represent a novel model for studying the role of mitochondria in the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes and neurodegeneration.

the molecular profile of the CRI-G1 cell line is a good representation for pancreatic β cells and that the CRI-G2-RS cell line may be a good experimental model for studying β cell dysfunction in type 2 diabetes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, at the cellular level, the ability to cope with mitochondrial dysfunction is not a binary trait.

differential vulnerability to mitochondrial and oxidants among different cell types is not simply a matter of differential ATP production/utilization, but rather is associated with differential regulation of a set of genes and pathways that are involved in the cellular stress response.

differential vulnerability to mitochondrial stress among different cell types may reflect differential regulation of antioxidant genes and that such regulation may be a key factor in determining the fate of cells in response to mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress.
